f1.quote: Atmospheric plasma spraying was used to deposit an approximately 150 µm-thick AlCoCrFeNi HEA coating on SS316L

f2.quote: followed by 2 h furnace annealing at 400, 550, 700, or 850 °C. The 550 °C condition was selected for corrosion testing because it produced the best reported microstructure and microhardness.

f3.quote: Electrochemical testing used 3.5 wt% H2SO4 with saturated calomel reference and Pt counter electrodes.

f4.quote: Hot-corrosion testing was conducted at 900 °C for ten 5 h cycles (50 h total) under mixture A (75% Na2SO4/25% NaCl), B (70% Na2SO4/20% NaCl/10% V2O5), or C (60% Na2SO4/20% NaCl/20% V2O5).

f5.quote: At 550 °C, annealing produced a dense, refined grain structure with an average grain size near 15 µm, approximately 80% more low-angle than high-angle grain-boundary fraction, fewer voids, and retained major BCC/minor FCC phases.

f6.quote: Grain refinement and the major BCC phase impede dislocation motion and increase hardness.

f7.quote: rapid formation of stable Al- and Cr-rich passive oxides restrict pit and crack development and impede sulphide attack.

f8.quote: During corrosion, Al-, Cr-, Fe-, and Co-containing oxide/hydroxide passive layers formed, including Cr2O3, Fe(OH)3, Cr(OH)3, and Co(OH)2. Under molten salts, the coating and oxide scale delay penetration and fluxing, although chloride, sulphide, and vanadate species can enter coating micropores and

f9.quote: Relative to uncoated SS316L and the as-sprayed coating, the AlCoCrFeNi-coated specimen annealed at 550 °C should exhibit greater microhardness... Annealing above 550 °C should reduce hardness because of grain growth, softening, and increased FCC/sigma-phase effects.
